pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Citrus blight is a wilt-and-decline disease of citrus, and its cause has not been determined.

affected_parts.quote: mild wilting and grayish cast to the foliage ... extensive twig dieback ... presence of amorphous plugs in the xylem ... presence of blight-associated citrus proteins in roots and leaves

summary.value: Mild wilting and a grayish cast to the foliage, often with zinc deficiency symptoms, followed by rapid decline with extensive twig dieback, off-season flowering, and small fruit; vegetative sprouts may develop on the trunk or interior branches.
summary.quote: The first symptoms on huanglongbing (HLB)-free trees are usually a mild wilting and grayish cast to the foliage, often accompanied by zinc deficiency symptoms on trees. Trees rapidly decline with extensive twig dieback, off-season flowering, and small fruit.

diagnostic_features.value: High zinc content in trunk bark and wood; amorphous plugs in the xylem; failure to absorb water injected into the trunk (blighted trees accept less than 0.5 ml in 10 seconds vs. at least 3 ml for healthy trees); and presence of blight-associated citrus proteins in roots and leaves.
diagnostic_features.quote: Citrus blight is characterized by (1) high zinc content in trunk bark and wood; (2) presence of amorphous plugs in the xylem; (3) failure to absorb water injected into the trunk; and (4) presence of blight-associated citrus proteins in roots and leaves.

look_alikes.quote: Blight symptoms can be confused with other decline diseases (e.g., HLB, tristeza decline, etc.) ... Healthy trees or trees declining from phytophthora root rot, nematodes, water damage, tristeza, or HLB will usually take up about 10 ml of water in 30 seconds.

conflicts.canonical_value: Foliar, Stem, Root, Vascular, Whole plant
conflicts.alternative_value: Foliar, Stem, Vascular, Whole plant (no Root listed)
conflicts.note: The EDIS HS241 source does not explicitly list Root among affected parts, whereas CG038 includes roots via reference to blight-associated proteins in roots.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: blue mold, caused by Penicillium italicum Wehmer, result in substantial economic losses around the globe

type_of_disease.quote: Blue and green mold fungi are mainly problems during fruit storage but can also occur on injured fruit on the tree.

affected_parts.quote: Blue and green mold fungi are mainly problems during fruit storage but can also occur on injured fruit on the tree.

summary.value: Infection initially appears as a circular, soft, water-soaked lesion on rinds (clear rot); spores of P. italicum are encapsulated in narrow white mycelium bounded by fluffy, water-soaked rind; the white mycelium grows into infected tissue and sporulates blue conidia, producing a watery soaked, soft and discolored fruit.
summary.quote: Spores of P. italicum are encapsulated in narrow white mycelium bounded by fluffy, water-soaked rind (Holmes and Eckert, 1999 ; Palou et al., 2002a , b , 2008 ; Talibi et al., 2014 ; Papoutsis et al., 2019 ). The white mycelium grows and digs into the infected tissue, sporulating blue conidia

diagnostic_features.value: Narrow white mycelium bounded by fluffy, water-soaked rind with blue sporulating conidia; a nesting-type pathogen that spreads rapidly in packed containers to infect adjacent fruits; white mycelium grows and extends deeper into infected tissue before sporulating into blue conidia.
diagnostic_features.quote: P. italicum is a nesting-type pathogen that spreads rapidly in packed containers to infect adjacent fruits (Ladaniya, 2008 ) even at lower temperatures in cold storage

look_alikes.quote: Blue mold ( Penicillium italicum ) and green mold ( P. digitatum ) usually occur together.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Green mold, caused by Penicillium digitatum Sacc, and blue mold, caused by Penicillium italicum Wehmer, result in substantial economic losses around the globe

type_of_disease.quote: P. digitatum , a necrotrophic fungus infecting citrus species via mechanical wounds and environmental factors such as cold, wind, insects, and hail, accounts for ~90% of total post-harvest losses alone

affected_parts.quote: Blue and green mold fungi are mainly problems during fruit storage but can also occur on injured fruit on the tree.

summary.value: The infected fruit produces white mycelia and greenish conidia; the mycelium breaks down fruit cell walls causing shrinkage into a sunken mummified form; infected pericarp and mesocarp cells plasmolyze, causing a soft watery spot and rotting the fruit; initial symptoms appear as a circular, soft, water-soaked lesion on the rind (clear rot).
summary.quote: The infected fruit then produces white mycelia and greenish conidia, a characteristic symptoms of green mold (Lin et al., 2019 ). The mycelium produces enzymes that break down fruit cell walls and initiate shrinkage, resulting in a sunken mummified form (Papoutsis et al., 2019 ). The infected pericarp and mesocarp cells plasmolyze, causing a soft watery spot, and the fruit is rotted

diagnostic_features.value: A thick non-sporulating mycelium limited by decaying peel surrounds green mold spores, distinguishing it from blue mold; initial lesions resemble blue mold but the surrounding thick white mycelium band is characteristic of green mold.
diagnostic_features.quote: Although initial lesions caused by green mold resemble blue mold disease, a thick non-sporulating mycelium limited by decaying peel surrounds green mold spores

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Huanglongbing (HLB; citrus greening) is thought to be caused by the bacterium, Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus.

type_of_disease.quote: HLB; citrus greening) is thought to be caused by the bacterium, Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus.

affected_parts.quote: The disease affects all parts of the tree canopy - leaves, twigs and fruit As the disease progresses, it will cause the whole tree to decline

summary.value: Early symptoms are vein yellowing and an asymmetrical chlorosis (blotchy mottle) on leaves; affected trees show twig dieback, yellow shoots, and stunting. Fruit are often small, lopsided, fail to color properly (remain green at the stylar end), may have a curved central core, aborted seeds, and a salty bitter taste.
summary.quote: The early symptoms of HLB on leaves are vein yellowing and an asymmetrical chlorosis referred to as \'blotchy mottle.\'

diagnostic_features.value: Blotchy mottle — an asymmetrical random pattern of yellowing (chlorosis) on leaves that is not the same on the right and left sides of the leaf — is the most diagnostic symptom, especially on sweet orange. A yellow stain may be present just beneath the peduncle (stem) on a cut fruit, and fruit often remain green at the stylar end with a curved central core.
diagnostic_features.quote: The blotchy mottle symptom is the most diagnostic symptom of the disease, especially on sweet orange.

look_alikes.quote: The blotchy mottle symptom also may be confused with other diseases or damage such as severe forms of citrus tristeza virus (CTV), Phytophthora root rot, water logging, citrus blight, leafminer tunnels or stubborn, a disease that is not known to be present in Florida.

summary.value: A postharvest disease on citrus fruit similar to blue mold, but distinguished by the formation of whisker-like coremia.
summary.quote: stored fruits of the medium-to-late-ripening citrus variety Shiranuhi ([ Citrus unshiu × C. sinensis ] × C. reticulata ) were found to have a disease similar to blue mold. The fungus causing this disease differed distinctly from the well-known, blue mold agent, Penicillium italicum, because it formed whisker-like coremia measuring 1–8 mm.

diagnostic_features.value: Formation of whisker-like coremia measuring 1–8 mm, distinguishing it from blue mold caused by Penicillium italicum.
